title: Trust registry — who may issue, which keys were theirs, and when this snapshot was true
description:
Governs content/trust-registry.yaml. Steward-controlled: admitting an issuer is a reserved decision under GOVERNANCE.md §5.

THE PROMISE THIS SERVES, AND THE ONE IT CANNOT KEEP. Decision 22 says verification is a signature check against a signed issuer trust registry distributed as a FILE — no ledger, no network, no call to the issuer. Air-gapped is the default. But a file is a SNAPSHOT, and an air-gapped verifier holds whatever snapshot reached them. A hiring manager on a closed network with last month's USB cannot learn that an issuer key was compromised last week.

'No network' and 'fresh trust' cannot both be absolute. That is not a defect to engineer away — it is a property of air-gapped operation, and any design claiming otherwise is lying about one of the two. So the registry does not attempt freshness. It makes STALENESS MEASURABLE: every snapshot states when it was issued and when the next was due, so a verifier can always answer 'how old is what I am trusting, and what could have happened since'. A verification result that does not carry its own age is the actual defect, and it was the one shipped.

KEYS ARE APPEND-ONLY WITHIN AN ISSUER, for the same reason element IDs are. A key removed from this file breaks every credential legitimately signed with it, including ones signed years before anything went wrong. Compromise is recorded by STATUS AND DATE, never by deletion — see `status` on a key, which is what lets a compromised key invalidate the signatures that followed the compromise while leaving the ones that preceded it standing.

issuedOn.description: When this snapshot was cut. THE MOST IMPORTANT FIELD IN THE FILE for an air-gapped verifier: everything they conclude is a statement about the world as it stood on this date, and a verifier that does not surface it is presenting a month-old answer as a current one.

sequence.description: Monotonically increasing snapshot number. Lets a verifier holding two copies tell which is newer without comparing dates, and lets a deployment detect that it has been fed an older snapshot than one it already had — the rollback a courier or a mirror can perform without touching the signature.

nextExpectedUpdate.description: When the next snapshot was expected. This is what converts 'old' from a feeling into a fact: past this date the verifier knows it is operating on a registry that should have been replaced, and can say by how many days. It is not an expiry — an overdue registry is still the best available truth in an air gap, and refusing to verify against it would strand exactly the deployments this design exists for.

didMethods.description:
The DID methods this deployment's verifiers can actually resolve, stated as a PROFILE. The credential schema deliberately does not fix a method, because the Personal edition must work with no server and no registrar. That freedom collides with offline verification: an arbitrary method may need a network resolver, so a credential could be schema-valid and unverifiable by the very verifier the design promises.

A deployment claiming offline verification lists here only methods whose verification material is self-contained (`did:key`) or travels with this file. Anything else is a credential the advertised verifier cannot resolve, and the validator rejects it rather than letting the promise quietly fail at the worst moment.

issuers.description: Admitted issuers. May be empty, which means no issuer has been admitted and no credential verifies — the correct state while steward appointment is outstanding.

entry.description: The key a credential names in `issuer.trustRegistryEntry`. Stable for the life of the issuer.

removedOn.description: When the issuer left the registry. The ENTRY IS NOT DELETED, because credentials they issued while admitted remain valid and a verifier must still be able to resolve them. Removal stops new issuance; it does not retroactively unmake old attestations.

accreditationRecognition.description: The issuer's own accreditation, where they hold one. Recorded here as well as on the credential so a verifier can check the claim against the registry rather than taking the credential's word for it — the `accredited-body` provenance tier rests on this.

keys.description: Every key this issuer has ever used, in order. APPEND-ONLY: a key is never removed, because removing it breaks every credential signed with it, including ones signed long before anything went wrong.

status.description:
THE DISTINCTION ITEM 8 TURNS ON. `retired` is ordinary rotation: the key signs nothing new after `retiredOn`, and everything it signed before remains valid — that is the whole point of rotating rather than revoking. `compromised` means the key fell into someone else's hands, and signatures dated from `compromisedFrom` onward cannot be trusted; signatures BEFORE that date are still good, because the key was still the issuer's when they were made.

Collapsing these two into 'revoked' would either keep trusting a stolen key or destroy years of legitimate credentials, and both are worse than the distinction being slightly fiddly.

compromisedFrom.description: The earliest date from which this key cannot be trusted. REQUIRED when status is `compromised`. Where the date of compromise is genuinely unknown, the honest entry is the key's own `validFrom`, which invalidates everything it ever signed — that is the conservative answer and it should be uncomfortable, because it is what not knowing actually costs.

revocations.description:
Credentials revoked by their issuers. Carried in this file because that is what 'a status list a verifier can obtain without contacting the issuer' means when the registry is the distribution channel — a separate endpoint would reintroduce the network call the whole design removes.

A revocation reaches an air-gapped verifier no faster than the registry does, which is the same staleness bound as everything else here and is stated rather than hidden.

proof.description: The registry is itself signed, or it is a text file anybody can edit on the way to the air gap.
